questions.question: What is R2DBC, and how do you use it correctly with Spring Data?
questions.title: R2DBC — Reactive Relational Data Access with Spring
questions.direct_answer: **R2DBC** (Reactive Relational Database Connectivity) is a non-blocking alternative to JDBC, with drivers for Postgres, MySQL, H2, MSSQL, MariaDB, and Oracle. You consume it through **Spring Data R2DBC** — `ReactiveCrudRepository`, `R2dbcEntityTemplate`, `DatabaseClient`. R2DBC is **not** JPA: no lazy loading, no first-level cache, no automatic relationships, no rich criteria API. Transactions work via the auto-configured **`R2dbcTransactionManager`** plus `@Transactional` or `TransactionalOperator`. Pick R2DBC when you are reactive-all-the-way and need streaming queries or genuine non-blocking I/O. In 2026, **MVC + virtual threads + JDBC** is a strong default; R2DBC earns its place for reactive WebFlux services and streaming row pipelines.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of reactive DB access, limitations vs JPA, transaction semantics, and modern alternatives (virtual threads)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating R2DBC like JPA; mixing R2DBC with JPA carelessly; not propagating reactive transaction context
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss r2dbc-postgresql LISTEN/NOTIFY streaming, connection pool tuning, reactive transaction propagation, Flyway migration coexistence

sections.title: What R2DBC Is — and Just as Importantly, What It Isn't
sections.content:
**R2DBC** is a specification (originated at Pivotal / VMware) for reactive database drivers over TCP. It exposes `Publisher<T>`-based APIs for connection, query, and transaction lifecycle, and it has mature drivers for the major SQL engines: r2dbc-postgresql, r2dbc-mysql, r2dbc-mssql, r2dbc-h2, r2dbc-mariadb, and r2dbc-oracle.

**Spring Data R2DBC** sits on top and provides three idiomatic entry points: `ReactiveCrudRepository` for declarative repositories, `R2dbcEntityTemplate` for fluent programmatic CRUD, and `DatabaseClient` for fluent SQL with parameter binding.

**What R2DBC is NOT:**
- Not JPA / Hibernate — no auto-flush, no first-level cache, no lazy loading
- Not a full ORM — relationships are explicit; you fetch and assemble
- No `@OneToMany` / `@ManyToMany` automatic loading
- No second-level cache
- No criteria API as rich as JPA's
- Limited batching compared to Hibernate

**What R2DBC IS:**
- Non-blocking, reactive database access
- Native integration with Reactor and WebFlux — queries return `Mono<T>` / `Flux<T>`
- True streaming — `Flux<Row>` over millions of rows without loading them all
- Reactive transactions via `R2dbcTransactionManager`
- Backpressure-aware at the driver level

sections.title: Non-Blocking DB Call Sequence
sections.content:
```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Ctl as Controller (Mono) participant Repo as ReactiveCrudRepository participant Tpl as R2dbcEntityTemplate participant Drv as r2dbc-postgresql driver participant EL as Netty event loop participant DB as PostgreSQL Ctl->>Repo: findById(42) Repo->>Tpl: select query Tpl->>Drv: createStatement / execute Drv->>EL: write SQL frame (non-blocking) EL->>DB: TCP send Note right of EL: thread is free
handles other requests DB-->>EL: rows arrive EL-->>Drv: read response frame Drv-->>Tpl: emit Row Tpl-->>Repo: map to entity Repo-->>Ctl: Mono onNext + onComplete ```

sections.title: Setup and Repository Pattern
Transactions, DatabaseClient, and Relationships
Limitations, Pitfalls, and the 2026 Decision Guide
sections.content:
**Limitations to know:**
- **No lazy loading or auto-fetch** — explicit joins or follow-up queries
- **No first-level cache** — two `findById(1)` calls hit DB twice
- **Limited batching** vs Hibernate
- **Streaming LOBs** support varies by driver
- **Migrations still use JDBC** — Flyway and Liquibase have no reactive versions; keep JDBC config for schema
- **`@Transactional` semantics differ** — reactive context must flow through the chain; mixing blocking and reactive breaks it
- **Error message** *Transaction not available in reactive context* usually means missing context propagation or wrong tx manager

**Common pitfalls:**
- **Mixing JPA and R2DBC entities** — possible but complex; usually pick one
- **R2DBC for complex OLTP with many relationships** — JPA is still better
- **Not using `r2dbc-pool`** — connection acquisition becomes the bottleneck
- **Wrong isolation level** — set via `spring.r2dbc.properties.isolation-level`
- **Query logging** requires driver-level flags, not just Spring Data settings
- **Pagination** — `Pageable` works; `.count()` is a separate query

**Connection pool sizing:**
- Start with `max-size = (2 × CPU_count) + effective_spindle_count` (same rule of thumb as JDBC)
- Monitor `r2dbc.pool.acquired.count` and `pending.count`
- Too small: requests queue for connections
- Too large: DB pressure; watch Postgres `max_connections`

**R2DBC vs JDBC + virtual threads — comparison**

| Aspect | R2DBC | JDBC + Virtual Threads |
|---|---|---|
| Non-blocking | Yes natively | Yes via Loom |
| JPA support | No | Yes |
| Relationships | Manual | Automatic (JPA) |
| Migrations | JDBC still required | Native |
| Learning curve | High | Low |
| Streaming rows | Excellent (Flux) | Possible with stream queries |
| Transaction propagation | Reactive context | ThreadLocal (normal) |
| Memory per connection | Low | Low (with VT) |
| Team familiarity | Lower | Higher |

**When R2DBC wins:**
- **Streaming millions of rows** with backpressure end-to-end
- **WebFlux app fully reactive** — DB is the missing piece
- **Simple CRUD** without complex relationships
- **Real-time streaming** scenarios (Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY via r2dbc-postgresql)

**When JDBC + virtual threads wins:**
- **Complex domain** with relationships and aggregates
- **Heavy JPA usage** — caching, lazy loading, criteria queries
- **Team unfamiliar** with reactive
- **Tooling maturity** matters — debuggers, profilers, ORMs, migrations
- **Most CRUD workloads**

**Testing**
- `@DataR2dbcTest` slices the context to data layer
- Testcontainers Postgres for realistic integration tests
- `StepVerifier` for chain assertions

```java
@DataR2dbcTest
class OrderRepositoryTest {
    @Autowired OrderRepository repo;

    @Test
    void saveAndFind() {
        StepVerifier.create(repo.save(new Order(null, 1L, "NEW", TEN, now())))
            .expectNextMatches(o -> o.id() != null)
            .verifyComplete();
    }
}
```

**Observability**
- Micrometer metrics — `r2dbc.pool.*`, query timing
- OpenTelemetry R2DBC instrumentation for distributed tracing
- Slow-query logging via driver config

**The 2026 recommendation:**
- **Default** — Spring MVC + virtual threads + JPA / JDBC; normal blocking code, scale via Loom
- **R2DBC sweet spot** — reactive WebFlux service, streaming queries, real-time patterns (LISTEN/NOTIFY), explicit backpressure on huge result sets
- **Don't** — pick R2DBC "for performance" vs JDBC + virtual threads without a streaming or reactive-all-the-way motivation

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **R2DBC** = reactive JDBC alternative; drivers for Postgres, MySQL, H2, SQL Server, MariaDB, Oracle
- **Spring Data R2DBC** provides `ReactiveCrudRepository`, `R2dbcEntityTemplate`, `DatabaseClient`
- **Not JPA** — no lazy loading, no first-level cache, manual relationships, limited batching
- **`@Transactional` works** with the auto-configured `R2dbcTransactionManager`
- **Migrations still JDBC** — Flyway and Liquibase have no reactive flavor
- **Streaming queries** — `Flux<Row>` over millions of rows without loading all into memory
- **Connection pool** via `r2dbc-pool`; tune like JDBC HikariCP
- **Use R2DBC when** streaming rows, WebFlux reactive-all-the-way, Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY
- **Use JDBC + virtual threads when** complex domain, JPA features needed, team familiar with blocking
- **Architectural decision**, not a performance tweak

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
R2DBC is Reactive Relational Database Connectivity — a non-blocking alternative to JDBC with drivers for Postgres, MySQL, H2, SQL Server, MariaDB, and Oracle. You consume it through Spring Data R2DBC.

**Three entry points**
- `ReactiveCrudRepository` — declarative repositories
- `R2dbcEntityTemplate` — fluent programmatic CRUD
- `DatabaseClient` — fluent SQL with parameter binding

**What it is NOT**
- Not JPA / Hibernate — no auto-flush, first-level cache, lazy loading
- Not a full ORM — relationships are explicit; you fetch and assemble
- No automatic `@OneToMany` loading
- No second-level cache
- Limited batching

**What it IS**
- Non-blocking, reactive DB access
- Native Reactor / WebFlux integration — `Mono<T>` / `Flux<T>`
- True streaming — `Flux<Row>` over millions of rows without loading them all
- Reactive transactions via `R2dbcTransactionManager`
- Backpressure-aware at driver level

**Transactions**
- `@Transactional` works; auto-configured `R2dbcTransactionManager`
- All operations in the chain run in one reactive transaction
- Programmatic alternative — `TransactionalOperator` plus `.as(tx::transactional)`
- Mixing blocking and reactive in a transaction breaks context propagation

**Migrations**
- Flyway and Liquibase don't have reactive versions
- Keep a JDBC URL just for migrations; runtime queries use R2DBC

**Connection pool**
- `r2dbc-pool` is essential
- Sizing rule of thumb the same as JDBC: `(2 × CPU) + spindle_count`
- Watch Postgres `max_connections`

**R2DBC vs JDBC + virtual threads**
- Both are non-blocking
- R2DBC: no JPA, manual relationships, JDBC migrations, high learning curve
- JDBC + virtual threads: full JPA, automatic relationships, native migrations, low learning curve
- R2DBC better for streaming and LISTEN/NOTIFY
- JDBC + VT better for complex domains and most CRUD

**When R2DBC wins**
- Streaming millions of rows with backpressure
- WebFlux fully reactive — DB is the missing piece
- Simple CRUD without complex relationships
- Real-time streaming via Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY

**The 2026 recommendation**
- Default — MVC + virtual threads + JPA / JDBC
- R2DBC sweet spot — reactive WebFlux, streaming queries, LISTEN/NOTIFY, explicit backpressure on huge result sets
- Don't pick R2DBC "for performance" without a streaming or reactive-all-the-way motivation

**Strategic answer**
- R2DBC is reactive DB access, not a JPA replacement
- Architectural decision, not a performance tweak
- Pick for streaming and reactive-all-the-way
- JDBC + virtual threads covers most cases

questions.question: R2DBC vs JDBC — feature-by-feature comparison and decision guide
questions.title: R2DBC vs JDBC — Reactive vs Blocking Database Access
questions.direct_answer: **JDBC** is the classic blocking SQL API — every query parks the calling thread until the database responds. **R2DBC** is the reactive, non-blocking equivalent — queries return `Mono` / `Flux` and the calling thread is free while the network round-trip happens. JDBC has 25 years of tooling — JPA, Hibernate, Spring Data JPA, every connection pool, every migration tool, every monitoring agent. R2DBC has none of JPA's caching or relationship management. With **virtual threads** (JDK 21+), JDBC code runs on cheap virtual threads that park on blocking I/O without blocking carriers — closing much of the original concurrency gap. Today the choice is rarely about raw throughput — it's about whether you're running reactive end-to-end or whether you need JPA's ORM features.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming R2DBC is always faster than JDBC; ignoring the JPA-feature gap; forgetting that migrations still need JDBC even with R2DBC
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss connection pool tuning differences, streaming row patterns, transaction semantics, and how virtual threads close the gap

sections.title: JDBC and R2DBC — Same Goal, Opposite Threading Models
sections.content:
**JDBC** has been the standard Java DB API since 1997.
- Every query method (`Statement.execute`, `PreparedStatement.executeQuery`, `Connection.commit`) blocks the calling thread until the database responds.
- Around it Java has built every major ORM (Hibernate, MyBatis, jOOQ), every connection pool (HikariCP, Tomcat JDBC), and every migration tool (Flyway, Liquibase).

**R2DBC** is the non-blocking equivalent — same SQL, same protocols, but the API returns `Publisher<T>` instead of blocking. The calling thread is free while the network round-trip happens. The driver uses Netty under the hood and reactive backpressure to control row delivery.

The **threading model** is the deepest difference. JDBC scales by adding threads; the practical limit on a typical service is the connection pool size (10-50 connections) and the thread pool size (200). R2DBC scales by sharing a handful of event-loop threads across thousands of in-flight queries.

**With virtual threads (JDK 21+)** the picture shifted dramatically.
- JDBC calls running on virtual threads still block, but they block a virtual thread — which parks cheaply and frees the carrier thread for other work. The OS-thread limit no longer applies.
- This closes much of the historical concurrency gap and makes JDBC + virtual threads a serious alternative for many services that previously would have been forced to R2DBC.

sections.title: Feature-by-Feature Comparison
sections.content:
Each row is a real engineering decision; the rightmost column flags how virtual threads change the equation.

| Dimension | JDBC | R2DBC | Virtual Threads Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| API style | Blocking | Reactive (`Mono`/`Flux`) | JDBC blocking is now cheap |
| Threading | Thread-per-query | Event-loop sharing | JDBC scales further with VT |
| ORM support | JPA, Hibernate, MyBatis, jOOQ | None of these | Unchanged |
| Caching | First-level + L2 (JPA) | None | Unchanged |
| Relationships | Automatic with JPA | Manual | Unchanged |
| Lazy loading | Yes (JPA) | No | Unchanged |
| Migrations | Flyway / Liquibase native | Flyway via JDBC URL | Unchanged |
| Streaming rows | `ResultSet.fetchSize` + cursor | `Flux<Row>` natural | R2DBC still cleaner |
| Backpressure | None | Native | R2DBC still wins |
| Transactions | `ThreadLocal`-bound | Reactive context | VT keeps `ThreadLocal` working |
| Connection pool | HikariCP | r2dbc-pool | Same sizing rules |
| Tooling maturity | 25+ years | ~5 years | JDBC tooling unchanged |
| Learning curve | Low | High | VT keeps JDBC easy |
| Best for | Most workloads, JPA-heavy | WebFlux + streaming | VT favors JDBC for most |

sections.title: Same Query Two Ways
Streaming, Transactions, and Pool Tuning
sections.content:
**Streaming rows**
- JDBC needs server-side cursors plus `ResultSet.fetchSize` to avoid loading everything
- R2DBC streams naturally — `Flux<Row>` with backpressure end-to-end

```java
// JDBC streaming: requires explicit fetchSize and a Stream
try (Stream<Order> stream = jdbc.queryForStream(
        "SELECT * FROM orders", new OrderRowMapper())) {
    stream.forEach(this::process);
}
```

```java
// R2DBC streaming: Flux is the contract
repo.findAll()
    .doOnNext(this::process)
    .subscribe();
```

**Transactions**
- JDBC: `@Transactional` with `DataSourceTransactionManager`; `ThreadLocal`-bound; compatible with virtual threads
- R2DBC: `@Transactional` with `R2dbcTransactionManager`; reactive context bound; only works inside the reactive chain

**Mixing blocking and reactive in one transaction is a footgun** — the boundary loses transaction context and you get partial commits.

**Connection pool tuning**
- HikariCP for JDBC, r2dbc-pool for R2DBC
- Same rule of thumb: `max = (2 × CPU) + effective_spindle_count`
- With virtual threads on JDBC, the pool becomes the real concurrency limit since virtual threads themselves are essentially free
- Tune `pendingAcquireTimeout` so requests fail fast rather than queue forever

**Migrations**
- Flyway and Liquibase have no reactive equivalents
- An R2DBC service still needs a JDBC URL just to run migrations at startup
- Don't try to write your own reactive migration tool — keep JDBC for schema

sections.title: When Each Wins, and the Pitfalls to Avoid
sections.content:
**When JDBC + virtual threads helps:**
- Standard CRUD with JPA features (caching, lazy loading, relationships)
- Existing codebase with extensive JPA / Hibernate use
- Complex transactional workflows that benefit from `ThreadLocal` semantics
- Team familiar with blocking imperative code
- Most modern services in 2026

**When R2DBC helps:**
- Reactive WebFlux service end-to-end
- Streaming queries — millions of rows with end-to-end backpressure
- Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY for real-time pub/sub
- Memory-constrained containers at extreme connection counts
- Reactive Kafka / Redis already in the pipeline

**Watch for — common pitfalls:**
- **Using `RestTemplate` or JDBC inside a WebFlux handler** — blocks the event loop and stalls every concurrent request
- **Mixing JPA and R2DBC entities** — possible but the cognitive load is huge; pick one per service
- **Believing R2DBC is faster** — at moderate concurrency the gap is often negligible; the win is in extreme connection counts and streaming
- **Over-tuning the connection pool with virtual threads** — virtual threads are free but DB connections are not; the pool is your real limiter
- **Forgetting Flyway needs JDBC** — you can't fully escape JDBC even on a reactive service
- **`@Transactional` on a method that returns `Mono` but uses `DataSourceTransactionManager`** — transactions don't propagate correctly across the reactive chain; need `R2dbcTransactionManager`

**Strategic choices in 2026:**
- Default to **JDBC + virtual threads + JPA** for new services on JDK 21+
- Choose **R2DBC** when streaming, reactive-all-the-way, or LISTEN/NOTIFY are real requirements
- Avoid mixing the two in one service unless you have a specific reason
- For an existing JPA codebase, virtual threads are a one-line config change with massive concurrency upside

**Pool sizing under virtual threads:**
- 10K virtual threads can each try to acquire a JDBC connection from a pool of 10 — most will block on `getConnection`
- Either size the pool larger or accept that the pool is your concurrency contract
- Set short `connectionTimeout` and clear failure semantics so callers fail fast rather than pile up

**Observability:**
- JDBC has decades of tooling — APM agents, query loggers, p6spy, Hibernate Statistics
- R2DBC tooling is catching up — Micrometer support, OpenTelemetry instrumentation, but still less mature
- For mission-critical services where deep DB observability matters, JDBC's tooling lead is real

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **JDBC** is blocking; **R2DBC** is reactive; both speak SQL to the same databases
- **Virtual threads (JDK 21+)** make JDBC blocking cheap — closing much of the concurrency gap
- **JPA, Hibernate, jOOQ, MyBatis** all run on JDBC; R2DBC has no equivalents
- **Streaming rows** is more natural in R2DBC; possible with JDBC via cursors and `fetchSize`
- **Transactions** — JDBC `ThreadLocal`-bound; R2DBC reactive-context-bound; mixing them is a footgun
- **Migrations** — Flyway and Liquibase still need JDBC even on R2DBC services
- **Connection pool** — HikariCP for JDBC, r2dbc-pool for R2DBC; same sizing rule of thumb
- **2026 default** — JDBC + virtual threads + JPA for most new services
- **R2DBC sweet spot** — reactive WebFlux, streaming, LISTEN/NOTIFY, explicit backpressure
- **Don't mix** the two in one service unless there's a specific reason

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
JDBC and R2DBC speak the same SQL to the same databases — the difference is the threading model and the ecosystem around them.

**JDBC**
- Blocking; every query parks the calling thread
- 25 years of tooling — JPA, Hibernate, every connection pool, every migration tool
- Scales by adding threads; pool size and thread pool are the limits
- With virtual threads (JDK 21+), blocking calls park cheaply and free the carrier — concurrency is no longer the wall it used to be

**R2DBC**
- Reactive, non-blocking; queries return `Mono` / `Flux`
- Calling thread is free during the network round-trip
- Native streaming — `Flux<Row>` with end-to-end backpressure
- No JPA equivalent; relationships are manual; no first-level cache
- Migrations still use JDBC — Flyway and Liquibase have no reactive flavor

**Transaction semantics**
- JDBC — `ThreadLocal`-bound; works with virtual threads
- R2DBC — reactive-context-bound; only works inside the reactive chain
- Mixing blocking and reactive across a transaction is a footgun

**When JDBC + virtual threads wins**
- Standard CRUD with JPA features
- Complex transactional workflows
- Team familiar with blocking code
- Most modern services in 2026

**When R2DBC wins**
- Reactive WebFlux end-to-end
- Streaming millions of rows with backpressure
- Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY pub/sub
- Reactive Kafka / Redis already in the pipeline

**Pitfalls**
- JDBC inside a WebFlux handler stalls the event loop
- Mixing JPA and R2DBC in one service is painful
- Believing R2DBC is faster — usually the gap is small at moderate concurrency
- Forgetting Flyway needs JDBC even on R2DBC
- `@Transactional` with the wrong tx manager doesn't propagate across reactive chains

**Strategic answer**
- The choice is rarely about raw throughput — it's about reactive-all-the-way vs JPA features
- Virtual threads have tilted the default back toward JDBC for most services
- Pick R2DBC for specific reasons — streaming, LISTEN/NOTIFY, reactive end-to-end — not by default

beats.text: When JDBC + virtual threads helps: Standard CRUD with JPA features (caching, lazy loading, relationships) Existing codebase with extensive JPA / Hibernate use Complex transactional workflows that benefit from ThreadLocal semantics Team familiar with blocking imperative code Most modern services in 2026 When R2DBC helps: Reactive WebFlux service end-to-end Streaming queries — millions of rows with end-to-end backpressure Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY for real-time pub/sub Memory-constrained containers at extreme connection counts Reactive Kafka / Redis already in the pipeline Watch for — common pitfalls: Using RestTemplate or JDBC inside a WebFlux handler.

JDBC has been the standard Java DB API since 1997. Every query method (Statement.execute, PreparedStatement.executeQuery, Connection.commit) blocks the calling thread until the database responds. Around it Java has built every major ORM (Hibernate, MyBatis, jOOQ), every connection pool (HikariCP, Tomcat JDBC), and every migration tool (Flyway, Liquibase). R2DBC is the non-blocking equivalent — same SQL, same protocols, but the API.
